records.name: Madagascar
records.summary_text:
Madagascar's trans visitors get legality without protection. Same-sex conduct between adults is legal from age 21 under the Penal Code, but the age of consent is unequal: same-sex acts involving someone under 21 remain offences, with Penal Code Article 331 attaching an indecent-assault band of five to ten years' imprisonment. There is no anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition, and no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, so a trans traveller — alone or with a partner — holds no local status and no named protection.

Practical safety is the dominant concern: LG

records.name: Comoros
records.summary_text: Comoros is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code criminalises acts “contrary to morality or against nature” (2 years), enforced: two women were detained in June 2024 after asking an Islamic preacher to marry them, convicted in December 2024 (released for time served). No LGR; small conservative archipelago.

sources.title: Comoros: Two Women Convicted of Same-Sex Intimacy

records.name: Mauritania
records.summary_text: Mauritania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 Penal Code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and Cairo 52 documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and Islamic-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system.
